newsitem.title: PERU: Peru upbeat despite rebels' rejection of asylum.
newsitem.headline: Peru upbeat despite rebels' rejection of asylum.

text.p: Peruvian officials remained upbeat on Tuesday about a peaceful solution to Lima's 11-week hostage siege despite a statement by Marxist rebels holding 72 men captive that rejected plans to grant them asylum abroad.

Congress President Victor Joy Way, a pro-government lawmaker, said Monday's eighth round of face-to-face talks between the government and Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels brought progress.
"As far as we know, there has been an advance where each side has outlined its position," Joy Way told local radio.
He added that President Alberto Fujimori's weekend trip to the Caribbean -- where he clinched an offer to grant the guerrillas asylum in Cuba -- had brought a bloodless end to the siege closer.
"In case the final decision reached implies an exit (from Peru) for the MRTA, he is working to facilitate that exit," said Joy Way, a member of Fujimori's Change 90-New Majority coalition.

But earlier on Tuesday, rebel chief Nestor Cerpa poured cold water on the asylum proposal, insisting the rebels want to stay in Peru and urging the government instead focus on their main demand of freedom for some 400 jailed comrades.

"Our first priority is to stay in our fatherland, which is the path we have chosen to fight at the side of our people," Cerpa said in a walkie-talkie conversation from within the captured Japanese ambassador's residence monitored by Reuters.
Cerpa specifically ruled out a rumoured asylum deal involving the Dominican Republic, but drew short of rejecting Cuban President Fidel Castro's offer of refuge made on Monday.
"We have no intention of looking for exile or asylum in the Dominican Republic, and even less in any country that oppresses its people," he said.

"With respect to the Cuban government's willingness to take us in, we consider it appropriate not to make a comment right now to avoid our words being distorted. We do this out of respect for the Cuban government, Commander Fidel Castro, his revolution and his people," he said.
In a surprise visit to Havana on Monday, Fujimori announced Castro's offer to accept the roughly 20 rebels holding the residence since Dec. 17.
Castro confirmed he would accept the MRTA fighters out of a "moral duty" and "not a question of convenience." The MRTA draws its inspiration from the 1959 Cuban revolution.

The proposal drew immediate backing from Tokyo, whose cooperation is essential to any solution. Japanese officials said Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto would seek support from the United States, an avowed enemy of Cuba, for the proposal.
Top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama insisted the plan would be an effective way to resolve the crisis.
"I will not say whether this is morally right or wrong," Kajiyama told a news conference. "I think it is an effective way both in terms of not giving in to terrorism and of ending this peacefully."
Cerpa, however, said Fujimori was creating "false expectations" with talk of asylum and diverting attention from the main issue of the MRTA prisoners.
The government has flatly ruled out any releases, although Fujimori has hinted at other concessions that analysts say might include improved prison conditions and trial processes.

Underscoring the rebels' rejection of asylum, Cerpa failed to turn up at Monday's eighth round of crisis talks in Lima, sending instead his No. 2 leader Rolly Rojas, who goes by the nom de guerre "El Arabe" -- The Arab.
Cerpa said the meeting between Rojas and government negotiator Domingo Palermo brought "no significant advances," although they had allowed for an open exchange of views.
Fujimori met Palermo and Japan's talks observer Terusuke Terada on Tuesday morning for a debriefing on talks, which are slated to continue on Wednesday.
